deep.reconstruction:
The page holds three separate research questions from Hilbert's problem notebook, continuing the list on the previous page. None contains a worked derivation.

(1) Equations for root-multiplicity patterns. Let f = a0 x^n + a1 x^{n-1} + ... + an, better written as a binary form f(x,y) = sum a_i x^{n-i} y^i. Hilbert asks for necessary and sufficient conditions that f have alpha equal roots, beta equal roots, and so on, i.e. a prescribed partition of n as the multiplicity pattern.
- The conditions must be pure equations (polynomial identities in the a_i), with no inequations.
- Hence a0 must stay a general coefficient and must not be normalised to 1. Setting a0 = 1 would silently impose the inequation a0 != 0.
- In modern terms (my gloss): the set of forms with multiplicity pattern at least lambda is a Zariski-closed subvariety of P^n, the coincident root locus X_lambda. The question asks for its defining ideal, or a generating set of it. If one dehomogenises with a0 = 1, one only sees the affine chart and loses the points where roots go to infinity.
- This is the general version of Hilbert's published 1886 Math. Ann. problem: covariant conditions for a binary form to be a perfect n-th power. That is the pattern (n), whose answer is that the Hessian vanishes identically.
- My illustration: for n = 2 the condition for a square is a0 a2 - a1^2 = 0, with middle coefficient written as 2a1. For n = 3, a triple root holds iff the three 2x2 minors of the catalecticant matrix [[a0,a1,a2],[a1,a2,a3]] vanish, with binomial coefficients. These equations correctly include the case a0 = 0 (root at infinity).

(2) Finite generation of 'quotient' rings. Hilbert states a theorem to be proved:
- Let R = k[f1,...,fm] be a finite integrity domain, i.e. a finitely generated ring of polynomial functions.
- Let phi1,...,phir be given forms.
- Claim: the set of all g/(phi^a) obtained by dividing those g in R that are divisible by power products of the phi_j again forms a finitely generated ring.
- In modern terms the object is roughly R' = R[1/phi1,...,1/phir] ∩ k[x1,...,xn]. Precisely, R' consists of polynomials h with h * phi^a in R for some monomial phi^a; this is one natural reading of 'divisible by powers and products … after division'.
- He defines 'endlicher Integritätsbereich' as polynomials (ganze rationale Funktionen) in finitely many such functions. He remarks that infinite, i.e. non-finitely generated, integrity domains also exist.
- This is the polynomial-ring analogue of the problem on the previous page: integer polynomials equal to F/p^n with F in Z[phi,psi,chi,...]. That page explicitly aims to recover the finiteness of invariants as a special case.

(3) Discriminant as a complete invariant. Take an equation with integer coefficients and allow rational (Tschirnhaus) transformations, which change the polynomial but not the generated field. The 'wesentliche Theiler' (essential divisor) of the discriminant is invariant under these. In modern language this is the field discriminant d_K, as opposed to the inessential index factor, with disc(f) = [O_K : Z[theta]]^2 d_K. Hilbert asks whether d_K is a sufficient (complete) invariant, i.e. whether it determines the equation up to rational transformation. The reference is to Hensel's work on essential and inessential discriminant divisors (Kronecker school, 1880s–90s).
errors: (2) As stated in full generality the 'Satz' is false. Rings of the form R[1/phi] ∩ k[x] with R finitely generated need not be finitely generated. Such intersections and saturations are exactly the shape of the counterexamples to Hilbert's 14th problem (Nagata 1959; Roberts 1990 via symbolic-type algebras). Hilbert gives no proof here; it is only stated as a goal. It does hold in important special cases, e.g. invariant rings of reductive groups.

(3) The answer to the question is negative beyond degree 2. The field discriminant does not determine the field up to isomorphism. Example: the two distinct cyclic cubic fields of conductor 63 both have discriminant 63^2 = 3969. Hilbert only poses the question, so this is not an error by him.
(1) No error. The methodological remark that a0 must be kept general so that only equations, not the inequation a0 != 0, are used is correct. It amounts to working projectively with binary forms.

results.what: Problem of finding purely equational (ideal-theoretic) necessary and sufficient conditions for a binary form to have a prescribed multiplicity pattern of roots, keeping a0 general.
results.modern_name: Defining equations / ideals of coincident root loci (Chow varieties of zero-cycles on P^1)
results.usually_credited_to: Perfect-power case: Hilbert 1886 (Math. Ann. 27), building on Brill/Gordan covariant methods. General loci: classical invariant theory (Brill, Gordan), modern work by Weyman, Chipalkatti, Abdesselam–Chipalkatti (2000s).

results.what: Conjectured theorem: if R is a finitely generated ring and phi_j are given forms, then the ring of quotients g/phi^a (g in R divisible by phi^a) is again finitely generated. Also the remark that non-finitely-generated integrity domains exist.
results.modern_name: Finite generation of R[1/phi] ∩ k[x]; a precursor of Hilbert's 14th problem
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert's 14th problem (1900); negative answer by Nagata (1959). Hilbert's 1890–93 finiteness theorems cover the invariant-theoretic special cases.

results.what: Question whether the essential discriminant divisor (field discriminant) is a complete invariant of an integral equation under rational transformation.
results.modern_name: Is the discriminant a complete invariant of a number field? (No for degree >= 3.) Discriminant = index^2 · field discriminant.
results.usually_credited_to: Kronecker and Hensel (essential/inessential discriminant divisors, 1880s–1894). Dedekind (field discriminant).

deep.surprise_reason: Items 1 and 3 are standard for the Kronecker/Hilbert circle; item 1 even overlaps Hilbert's own 1886 paper. Item 2 is a mildly notable early, pre-1900 formulation of a finite-generation question of exactly the type later posed as Hilbert's 14th problem. Hilbert states it as a theorem to prove, and it is false in general. This is an interesting genealogical detail but not a hidden result.

checkable.asserts: A perfect square binary quadratic satisfies a0*a2 - a1^2 = 0 (equational condition valid also when a0 = 0).

checkable.asserts: A cube of a linear form satisfies the vanishing of all 2x2 catalecticant minors (equivalently the Hessian vanishes identically), using only equations.
The cyclic cubic field of conductor 7 has polynomial discriminant 49 = 7^2, equal to the field discriminant (illustrating the essential discriminant divisor).
A rational (Tschirnhaus) transform t = 2x+1 of x^2-5 changes the polynomial discriminant by a square factor (index^2): disc becomes 80 = 4*20 while the field discriminant 5 is unchanged.
